name: Semax
used_for: A synthetic seven-amino-acid peptide derived from an ACTH fragment, developed in Russia. A secondary source (an encyclopedia page, not an official register) says it is on Russia's list of vital and essential drugs and is used there for conditions such as stroke; the same source says it is not FDA approved in the US. It is promoted online as a focus and memory aid. The human evidence found is small and Russian, with one non-placebo-controlled stroke-rehabilitation study; most other work is in rodents and cell models.

entries.text: Two courses of 6000 mcg per day for 10 days each, with a 20-day gap, were given in a stroke rehabilitation study (administration route not stated in the abstract). The study was not placebo-controlled.

administration_guidance.text: In a trial of 110 people after ischemic stroke, the standard Semax regimen was two courses of 10 days each, separated by a 20-day interval. The abstract does not state the route of administration.
administration_guidance.label: research

administration_guidance.text: A prescribing clinic's guide (Beverly Hills Rejuvenation Center) says Semax is usually dosed in the morning and early afternoon, with late-day use avoided to prevent sleep interference, that intranasal is the most common route, and that a reconstituted vial is kept refrigerated and used within a few weeks.
administration_guidance.label: internet

administration_guidance.text: A peptide information site (The Peptide Initiative, which states it sells no products) describes three routes for Semax (intranasal as the preferred one, or subcutaneous injection in the abdomen or outer thigh with sites rotated), says it can be used regardless of food, and says different nasal peptides are spaced 15 to 30 minutes apart.
administration_guidance.label: internet

side_effects.text: A prescribing clinic's guide (Beverly Hills Rejuvenation Center) lists nasal irritation, dryness or sting, mild headache, lightheadedness and fatigue as reported effects of Semax, plus overstimulation or sleep trouble when used late in the day, and notes long-term effects are unknown given limited human data.
side_effects.label: internet

internet_claims.claim: A Superpower guide says Semax is a Russian-developed peptide that may raise BDNF and NGF and may help stroke recovery and cognition, but notes the largest human study (110 stroke patients) was non-randomized and not placebo-controlled, and that it is not FDA approved.
Swolverine, a supplement retailer's blog, presents Semax as a focus-enhancing peptide that raises BDNF and cites Russian clinical data as support; the page is informational and does not sell Semax.

Nuusflits says Semax and Selank remain registered drugs in Russia but that the FDA has never reviewed them, and says FDA moved them to Category 1 for compounding in February 2026. The FDA page consulted instead lists them as nominated but withdrawn, so this claim could not be confirmed.

research.summary: Russian study (Zh Nevrol Psikhiatr Im S S Korsakova) of 110 patients after ischemic stroke, split by early or late rehabilitation and by whether they received Semax. Not randomized or placebo-controlled as described.
research.finding: Patients given Semax had higher blood BDNF levels and the authors report faster functional recovery on the Barthel index and better motor performance. Because groups were not placebo-controlled, this cannot show that Semax caused the improvement.

research.summary: Small brain-imaging study (Dokl Biol Sci) comparing resting-state fMRI connectivity before and after an injection of Semax, Selank or placebo in volunteers.
research.finding: Differences in connectivity between the right amygdala and right temporal regions were found after Semax and Selank. This is a brain-activity measure, not evidence of a clinical benefit.

research.summary: Rat study (Neuropeptides) of whether Semax could reverse behavioral and brain chemistry changes caused by early-life exposure to the antidepressant fluvoxamine.
research.finding: Semax reduced anxiety-like behavior, improved maze learning and normalized brain monoamine levels in the rats. Rat results do not establish effects in people.

research.summary: Mouse and cell study (Br J Pharmacol) of Semax after spinal cord injury in female mice, plus a PC12 cell model.
research.finding: Semax improved functional recovery in the injured mice and reduced markers of cell death in the models; the authors link this to the mu-opioid receptor. Animal and cell evidence only.

research.summary: Laboratory study (ACS Chem Neurosci) of Semax in artificial membrane models with amyloid beta and copper.
research.finding: Semax reduced copper-driven amyloid beta aggregation and related toxicity in test-tube models. It is not evidence for any effect in Alzheimer's disease in people.

research.summary: FDA web page on bulk drug substances nominated for compounding that may present significant safety risks (page dated 04/22/2026, fetched 2026-09-30).
research.finding: The page lists Semax among substances nominated but withdrawn (not in the active Category 2 list), with this FDA statement: "Compounded drugs containing semax (heptapeptide) may pose risk for immunogenicity for certain routes of administration due to the potential for aggregation and peptide-related impurities." The page does not make it an approved drug.
